page.overview:
What is You Know What to Do?

You Know What to Do is the second known solo composition by George Harrison after "Don't Bother Me" the previous year. A demo was recorded on 3 June 1964 at Studio Two, EMI Studios, the song's only known performance by the Beatles. It progressed no further and remained unreleased until Anthology 1 in 1995. Paul McCartney remarked upon its re-discovery that the song is "not the greatest thing that George ever wrote," but is nonetheless "an undiscovered nugget" and that "[i]f you find a little Egyptian pot, it doesn’t have to be the greatest Egyptian pot. The fact that it is Egyptian is enough." Critical reception after its released was muted to negative.

The afternoon and evening of 3 June 1964 had already been booked for recording before Ringo Starr fell ill with tonsillitis and pharyngitis at a photo shoot that morning. After the fact it was reported that these sessions had been "scheduled for vocal dual-tracking only", but some sources speculate that it may have been intended for recording a fourteenth song for A Hard Day's Night. This may be related to a comment Harrison made in an earlier interview on 28 April that he thought he might have a composition on the band's next LP.

The first hour of the session, from 3.00-4.00p, was devoted to rehearsing six songs with hastily found replacement drummer Jimmie Nicol. Afterward from 5.30p-9.30p, the three present Beatles took the opportunity to record. Before John Lennon taped a demo of "No Reply" intended for Tommy Quickly, Harrison performed "You Know What to Do". The song had been copyrighted the previous day by Jaep Music, a company formed by Dick James and Brian Epstein to which Harrison was contracted.

According to John C. Winn, Harrison sang and played guitar, with McCartney on bass guitar and Lennon on tambourine. Ian MacDonald, however, proposed that since "nothing on the surviving demo was unplayable" by Harrison, he may have been the sole contributor. The verses are based on standard I-IV-V chords in the key of A major, opening with the IV. The bridge features a truncated chromatic minor run (8-7), with the dissonant minor/major 7th chord, as a ii. Walter Everett saw the song as a precursor to "You Like Me Too Much", while also noting the bass guitar's "chromatic descent, B-Bb-A beneath the opening Bm chord" in the bridge, similar to "Got to Get You into My Life". However, since it then simply resolves back on the I chord, the bridge essentially "goes nowhere... dooming the song to disgrace".
